title: Precedence, Associativity and Sequence Points
quickIdea: Precedence and associativity decide how the compiler groups an expression. Sequence points decide whether the side effects inside it have an order at all - and where there is none, the program's output is undefined rather than merely uncertain.
remember: Precedence, high to low: [] and () ; postfix ++ -- ; prefix ++ -- and unary * & ! ~ and casts ; * / % ; + - ; << >> ; < <= > >= ; == != ; & ; ^ ; | ; && ; || ; ?: ; assignment, right to left ; comma.
Postfix ++ binds tighter than unary *, so *p++ is *(p++): it reads the current element and then advances the pointer. (*p)++ increments the element and leaves the pointer where it is.
&& and || short-circuit, so the right operand is not evaluated when the left decides the result. Bitwise & and | do not short-circuit and always evaluate both sides.

A sequence point is a full expression, the return from a function call, or the boundary between the three expressions of a for header. Between two sequence points an object may be modified at most once.
i++ + ++i and printf("%d %d", i++, i++) have no defined answer: the same object is modified twice, or modified and read, with no sequence point between the two.

example.prompt: int r() { static int num = 7; return num--; } int main() { for (r(); r(); r()) printf("%d", r()); } What is displayed?
example.work: Each call returns the current value and then decrements the single static num. The for header runs as: initialisation r() returns 7 (num 6); the test r() returns 6 (num 5) and is true, so the body runs and its printf prints the 5 returned by that r() call (num 4); the update r() returns 4 (num 3); the test r() returns 3 (num 2) and is true, so the body prints 2 (num 1); the update r() returns 1 (num 0); the test r() returns 0 (num -1) and is false, so the loop ends.
example.answer: 52 - two characters, printed in the order 5 then 2.

gateAngle: GATE CSE 2019 Q.27 is this program and the answer is 52. The marks are in the order the three for expressions run in, not in the static variable: each is a separate full expression, so the sequence is init, test, body, update, test, body, and so on. The same precedence fact decides the *p++ family of questions.

variations.label: ORIGINAL PYQ-STYLE QUESTION
variations.question: int a[] = {5, 8}; int *p = a; int u = *p++; int v = (*p)++; What are u, v and the array afterwards?
variations.answer: u = 5, v = 8, and a becomes {5, 9}: *p++ reads a[0] and then moves p to a[1], and (*p)++ returns the old a[1] and increments the element.
variations.why: The same precedence rule as the 2019 trace, asked directly instead of hidden inside a loop header.

variations.label: CONCEPTUAL PRACTICE QUESTION
variations.question: Is f(g(), h()) undefined because g and h may run in either order?
variations.answer: No. Each call is a complete function call and finishes before the other starts, so only the order is unspecified, and either order gives a defined result if g and h share no state. The undefined case is printf("%d %d", i++, i++), where two unsequenced modifications of one object meet.
variations.why: Separates unspecified order from undefined behaviour, a distinction every evaluation-order question depends on.

variations.label: PREDICTED VARIATION
variations.question: What does printf("%d", 1 + 2 * 3 - 4 / 2) print, and what does strict left-to-right evaluation of the same operands give?
variations.answer: 5 by precedence; left to right it would be ((1 + 2) * 3 - 4) / 2 = 5 / 2 = 2, which is the wrong answer.
variations.why: The arithmetic-precedence version of the same question, worth one mark on its own.

trap.what: Assuming that function arguments are evaluated left to right.
trap.why: The standard leaves the order of evaluation of a call's arguments unspecified, so the two conversions in printf("%d %d", i++, i++) may happen in either order - and because the two modifications of i are unsequenced, the program is undefined rather than 'one of the two'. A trace built on left-to-right order is a guess, not an answer.
trap.counterexample: printf("%d %d", i++, i++) with i = 5 has no required output at all, while printf("%d %d", i, i + 1) does, because nothing is modified.

check.question: What does *p++ do, and what does (*p)++ do?
check.answer: *p++ is *(p++): it yields the element p currently points at and then advances p by one element. (*p)++ yields that element's old value and increments the element, leaving p where it is.
check.explanation: Postfix ++ binds tighter than unary *, so the parentheses are exactly what changes the meaning.
